paragraphs.text: וַיַּ֣רְא יַעֲקֹ֔ב כִּ֥י יֶשׁ־שֶׁ֖בֶר בְּמִצְרָ֑יִם וַיֹּ֤אמֶר יַעֲקֹב֙ לְבָנָ֔יו לָ֖מָּה תִּתְרָאֽוּ׃

i18n.en: Now Ya'aqov saw that there was grain in Mitsrayim, and Ya'aqov said unto his sons, Why do ye look one upon another?

paragraphs.commentary:
The chapter's first sentence introduces two of its keywords. *Shever* (שֶׁבֶר), the chapter's grain-trade keyword, will recur eight times across vv 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 19, 25, 26 — the noun for grain-as-purchased-commodity, with the cognate verb *shavar* (Qal *lishbor*, 'to buy grain') and the Hiphil *mashbir* ('one who sells grain', v 6). The *shever*/*lishbor*/*mashbir* cluster is the technical grain-trade vocabulary of the entire Gen 41-47 famine-and-purchase arc; HALOT registers the lexeme's specialized commercial sense (distinct from *bar*, the threshed-grain noun used at v 3 and v 25, and from *dagan*, the generic 'cereal'). The cross-corpus reach (Isa 55:1; Amos 8:5; Prov 11:26; Neh 10:32) — all in grain-trade contexts — confirms the lexeme's commercial-keyword status. The ASV-baseline 'grain' / 'to buy grain' / 'sold' is preserved across all eight occurrences; the central entry [`shever-mashbir-grain-purchase-vocabulary-yosef-cycle`](#shever-mashbir-grain-purchase-vocabulary-yosef-cycle) governs the cluster.

*Titra'u* (תִּתְרָאוּ), Ya'aqov's opening rebuke, is the Hithpael of *ra'ah* ('to see') and a near-hapax in this sense — the reciprocal-reflexive 'look at one another' (HALOT s.v. *ra'ah* Hithpael). The ASV-baseline 'Why do ye look one upon another?' (with its implicit 'helplessly') is retained; the sharper 'why do ye stare at each other' (NJPS register) and the 'why do ye show yourselves / stand about' (Hithpael-as-display reading) are documented in the overlay entry as defensible alternatives. The clause carries Ya'aqov's exasperation: the sons know there is grain in Mitsrayim and yet do nothing.

See Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 290; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 pp. 105-106; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 515-516; on the *shever*/*lishbor* commercial vocabulary, see HALOT s.v. *shever* II and BDB p. 991.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֕אמֶר הִנֵּ֣ה שָׁמַ֔עְתִּי כִּ֥י יֶשׁ־שֶׁ֖בֶר בְּמִצְרָ֑יִם רְדוּ־שָׁ֙מָּה֙ וְשִׁבְרוּ־לָ֣נוּ מִשָּׁ֔ם וְנִחְיֶ֖ה וְלֹ֥א נָמֽוּת׃

i18n.en: And he said, Behold, I have heard that there is grain in Mitsrayim: get you down thither, and buy for us from thence; that we may live, and not die.

paragraphs.text: וַיֵּרְד֥וּ אֲחֵֽי־יוֹסֵ֖ף עֲשָׂרָ֑ה לִשְׁבֹּ֥ר בָּ֖ר מִמִּצְרָֽיִם׃

i18n.en: And Yosef's ten brethren went down to buy grain from Mitsrayim.

paragraphs.commentary: The verse pairs the verb *lishbor* (the Qal of *shavar*, 'to buy grain') with the object *bar* (בָּר, 'threshed grain / cereal'). The lexeme-distinction is precise: *bar* is the threshed kernel; *shever* (the chapter's keyword noun) is grain-as-purchasable-commodity. The shift from *shever* (vv 1, 2) to *bar* here is not a contradiction but a register-shift — Ya'aqov speaks of *shever* (the goods to be procured); the narrator describes the object being purchased as *bar* (the substance itself). The brothers number ten — Binyamin is held back (v 4), and Yosef is unknown to be alive; the deliberate ten-brother count primes the recognition-and-restoration arithmetic that the chapter's remainder will work out.

paragraphs.text: וְאֶת־בִּנְיָמִין֙ אֲחִ֣י יוֹסֵ֔ף לֹא־שָׁלַ֥ח יַעֲקֹ֖ב אֶת־אֶחָ֑יו כִּ֣י אָמַ֔ר פֶּן־יִקְרָאֶ֖נּוּ אָסֽוֹן׃

i18n.en: But Binyamin, Yosef's brother, Ya'aqov sent not with his brethren; for he said, Lest peradventure harm befall him.

paragraphs.commentary:
The narrator's *Binyamin, Yosef's brother* is pointed — of all the brothers, only Binyamin and the (presumed-dead) Yosef are sons of Rachel, and Binyamin is identified by the bond Ya'aqov believes to have been irrevocably broken. The phrase will recur (v 38, 'his brother is dead, and he only is left'); the chapter's grief-arithmetic places Binyamin as the last surviving Rachel-son.

*Ason* (אָסוֹן), 'harm / fatal mischance', is a marked term in the HB. Outside Exod 21:22-23 (the law of injury to a pregnant woman, where the term denotes a fatal injury), the lexeme is confined to Ya'aqov's mouth in the Yosef cycle (Gen 42:4, 38; 44:29) — a Ya'aqov-internal fear-formula for the calamity that might befall Binyamin on the journey. The Exodus parallel decisively fixes the lethal force of the term; the ASV-baseline 'harm' (modernized from the archaic KJV 'mischief', which has drifted in modern English toward 'misbehavior') is preserved. See HALOT s.v. *ason* and the overlay entry [`ason-fatal-mischance-yaaqov-fear-formula-gen42`](#ason-fatal-mischance-yaaqov-fear-formula-gen42); on the Exod 21:22 lethal-injury sense, see C. Houtman *Exodus* HCOT 1996, ad loc.

paragraphs.text: וַיָּבֹ֙אוּ֙ בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל לִשְׁבֹּ֖ר בְּת֣וֹךְ הַבָּאִ֑ים כִּֽי־הָיָ֥ה הָרָעָ֖ב בְּאֶ֥רֶץ כְּנָֽעַן׃

i18n.en: And the sons of Yisra'el came to buy among those that came: for the famine was in the land of Kena'an.

paragraphs.text: וְיוֹסֵ֗ף ה֚וּא הַשַּׁלִּ֣יט עַל־הָאָ֔רֶץ ה֥וּא הַמַּשְׁבִּ֖יר לְכָל־עַ֣ם הָאָ֑רֶץ וַיָּבֹ֙אוּ֙ אֲחֵ֣י יוֹסֵ֔ף וַיִּשְׁתַּֽחֲווּ־ל֥וֹ אַפַּ֖יִם אָֽרְצָה׃

i18n.en: And Yosef was the governor over the land; he it was that sold to all the people of the land: and Yosef's brethren came, and made obeisance to him with their faces to the earth.

paragraphs.commentary:
**This is the first fulfilment of Yosef's Gen 37:7 sheaves-dream.** The narrator names two of Yosef's office-titles in apposition (*hu ha-shallit al ha-aretz hu ha-mashbir le-khol am ha-aretz* — *he was the governor over the land; he it was that sold to all the people of the land*) and then records the brothers' prostration: *va-yavo'u achei Yosef va-yishtachavu-lo apayim artzah*, 'and Yosef's brethren came, and made obeisance to him with their faces to the earth'. The verb *va-yishtachavu* (וַיִּשְׁתַּחֲווּ) is the same Hishtaphel of *chwh* (formerly mis-parsed as Hithpael of *shachah*) that Gen 37:7, 9, 10 used three times of the sheaves, the sun-moon-stars, and Ya'aqov's incredulous response — and v 9 will immediately confirm the narrator's intention: *va-yizkor Yosef et ha-chalomot asher chalam lahem* ('and Yosef remembered the dreams which he dreamed of them'). The narrator-flagged dream-fulfilment is decisive.

The entry [`hishtachavah-bow-down-obeisance-worship`](#hishtachavah-bow-down-obeisance-worship) has been **promoted from the Genesis-WoH overlay to the central glossary** at this verse (carrying forward the Gen 37 anchor-verses and extending the appliesTo to include the fulfilment-arc — Gen 42:6 here, with the forward fulfilment-verses 43:26, 28; 44:14; 50:18 to be confirmed when those chapters are translated). The verb is one of the HB's commonest worship/homage verbs (hundreds of occurrences across the corpus, governing all the standard prostration / worship / obeisance-to-superior scenes); the central housing reflects this corpus-wide reach.

The two office-titles in apposition mark Yosef's *functional* dual role. *Shallit* (שַׁלִּיט) is the Aramaic-influenced Hebrew 'ruler / one having authority' — cognate to Aramaic *shlita*, with primary cross-corpus reach at Eccl 7:19; 8:8; 10:5 (the late-wisdom-Hebrew usage) and across the Aramaic-section Daniel court-narratives (Dan 2:10, 15; 5:7, 16, 29; 6:27). The 'governor' rendering preserves the ASV-baseline; the NJPS 'vizier' captures the Egyptian-court office (*t3ty*); Alter's 'regent' is a third option. See the central entry [`shallit-ruler-aramaic-influenced-governance-lexeme`](#shallit-ruler-aramaic-influenced-governance-lexeme).

*Mashbir* (מַשְׁבִּיר) is the Hiphil participle of *shavar*, paired with *shallit* as the political/administrative title's commercial counterpart — Yosef is both the *shallit* (ruler) and the *mashbir* (one who sells grain). The cluster is governed by the same central entry as the chapter's *shever* / *lishbor* keyword.

The brothers' *apayim artzah* ('with their faces to the earth') is the standard full-prostration formula (cf. Gen 19:1, 33:3; Num 22:31; 1 Sam 20:41, 25:23; 2 Sam 14:33; 1 Kgs 1:23, 31), distinct from a lesser bow.

See HALOT s.v. *chwh* (Hishtaphel) and *shallit*; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 290; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 pp. 106-107; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 516-517; on the dream-fulfilment structure, see G. W. Coats *From Canaan to Egypt* CBQMS 4, 1976.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּ֥רְא יוֹסֵ֛ף אֶת־אֶחָ֖יו וַיַּכִּרֵ֑ם וַיִּתְנַכֵּ֨ר אֲלֵיהֶ֜ם וַיְדַבֵּ֧ר אִתָּ֣ם קָשׁ֗וֹת וַיֹּ֤אמֶר אֲלֵהֶם֙ מֵאַ֣יִן בָּאתֶ֔ם וַיֹּ֣אמְר֔וּ מֵאֶ֥רֶץ כְּנַ֖עַן לִשְׁבָּר־אֹֽכֶל׃

i18n.en: And Yosef saw his brethren, and he knew them, but made himself strange unto them, and spake roughly with them; and he said unto them, Whence come ye? And they said, From the land of Kena'an to buy food.

paragraphs.commentary:
The chapter stages the recognition-motif at its culmination: in a single verse the root *nakar* (נכר) is deployed in two opposite stems back-to-back — the Hiphil *va-yakkirem* ('and he recognised them', the same Hiphil of recognition that *haker-na* used at Gen 37:32 and that *va-yakker* used at Gen 38:26) and the Hithpael *va-yitnakker* ('and he made himself strange / disguised himself / feigned to be a stranger'). The same Hithpael recurs only at 1 Kgs 14:5-6 (the woman disguising herself to the blind prophet Achiyah of Shilo) — also a recognition-and-disguise scene. The juxtaposition of the two stems within a single verse is rare and pointed: the verb of recognition is the very verb whose anti-form Yosef adopts to conceal himself.

The scene is the explicit measure-for-measure culmination of the *nakar*-recognition arc that Gen 27 (Ya'aqov's deception of the blind Yitzchaq), Gen 37:32-33 (the brothers' *haker-na* to Ya'aqov over the bloodied tunic), and Gen 38:25-26 (Tamar's *haker-na* to Yehudah over the pledge-items) have built. The brothers, who once exploited their father's misrecognition of a bloodied tunic — and stood by while Yehudah was caught in a *haker-na* by Tamar — are themselves now misrecognising the brother they sold. The role-reversal is exact: Yosef the once-recognised tunic-wearer now plays the unrecognised stranger.

The overlay entry [`haker-na-nakar-recognition-motif`](#haker-na-nakar-recognition-motif) has had its appliesTo extended to include this verse and v 8; a new sibling overlay entry [`nakar-hitnakker-recognition-feigning-gen42`](#nakar-hitnakker-recognition-feigning-gen42) records the paired Hiphil-and-Hithpael deployment that is specific to this chapter, with bidirectional cross-reference to the existing recognition-motif entry. The ASV-baseline 'knew them ... made himself strange unto them' is preserved (NJPS 'acted like a stranger'; Alter 'feigned to be a stranger'). 'Spake roughly' (*va-yedaber itam qashot*) — the adverbial-feminine-plural *qashot* ('hard / harsh things') is a known idiom for harsh speech; recurs at v 30 (the brothers' retelling).

See HALOT s.v. *nakar* (Hiphil and Hithpael); BDB p. 647; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 290; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 107; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 518; Alter *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 242 (on the recognition-motif); Alter *The Art of Biblical Narrative* 1981 ch. 1 (the foundational reading of the Gen 27 / 37 / 38 / 42 recognition-arc).

paragraphs.text: וַיַּכֵּ֥ר יוֹסֵ֖ף אֶת־אֶחָ֑יו וְהֵ֖ם לֹ֥א הִכִּרֻֽהוּ׃

i18n.en: And Yosef knew his brethren, but they knew not him.

paragraphs.commentary: The narrator's terse one-clause restatement (*va-yakker Yosef et echav ve-hem lo hikkiruhu*) drives the asymmetry into a single contrast: one brother recognises; the others do not. The repetition of the recognition-verb (Hiphil *yakker* and the negated Hiphil *hikkiruhu*) frames the entire Gen 42-45 sequence as a *delayed recognition*: it will not be resolved until Gen 45:1-4 (*ani Yosef achikhem* — 'I am Yosef your brother'). The intervening chapters work out, in slow time, the moral preconditions for that disclosure.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּזְכֹּ֣ר יוֹסֵ֔ף אֵ֚ת הַחֲלֹמ֔וֹת אֲשֶׁ֥ר חָלַ֖ם לָהֶ֑ם וַיֹּ֤אמֶר אֲלֵהֶם֙ מְרַגְּלִ֣ים אַתֶּ֔ם לִרְא֛וֹת אֶת־עֶרְוַ֥ת הָאָ֖רֶץ בָּאתֶֽם׃

i18n.en: And Yosef remembered the dreams which he dreamed of them, and said unto them, Ye are spies; to see the nakedness of the land ye are come.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Va-yizkor Yosef et ha-chalomot asher chalam lahem* — 'and Yosef remembered the dreams which he dreamed of them' — is the narrator's explicit pointer to the Gen 37:5-11 dream-pair: it is the brothers' prostration of v 6 that has triggered the recollection, and the narrator names the connection so the reader will not miss it. The Hebrew *chalam lahem* ('dreamed *to/of/for* them', with the lamed of regard) is faintly ambiguous between 'dreamed *about* them' and 'dreamed *to* them' (told them); both senses converge on the same Gen 37 referent.

Yosef's accusation deploys a marked idiom: *ervat ha-aretz* (עֶרְוַת הָאָרֶץ), literally 'the nakedness of the land'. The noun *ervah* ('nakedness, exposed/shameful part') is otherwise the Lev 18 / 20 sexual-shame term (*galah ervah*, 'uncover the nakedness of', the incest-prohibition formula) and the Deut 24:1 marital *ervat davar*. Here it is transferred to geopolitical sense — the land's undefended places, vulnerabilities, weak points (a spy's-eye view, looking for the gaps in the territorial fabric the way a man looks for what is shamefully uncovered). The literal preservation in ASV/KJV/NJPS/Alter ('the nakedness of the land') keeps the spy-trope intelligible. The idiom recurs at v 12 and is confined to this chapter within Genesis; the overlay entry [`ervat-ha-aretz-nakedness-of-the-land-spy-idiom-gen42`](#ervat-ha-aretz-nakedness-of-the-land-spy-idiom-gen42) governs the chapter-internal use, cross-referencing the Lev 18 / 20 sexual sense.

See HALOT s.v. *ervah*; BDB p. 788; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 290; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 pp. 107-108; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 519.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּאמְר֥וּ אֵלָ֖יו לֹ֣א אֲדֹנִ֑י וַעֲבָדֶ֥יךָ בָּ֖אוּ לִשְׁבָּר־אֹֽכֶל׃

i18n.en: And they said unto him, Nay, my lord, but to buy food are thy servants come.

paragraphs.text: כֻּלָּ֕נוּ בְּנֵ֥י אִישׁ־אֶחָ֖ד נָ֑חְנוּ כֵּנִ֣ים אֲנַ֔חְנוּ לֹא־הָי֥וּ עֲבָדֶ֖יךָ מְרַגְּלִֽים׃

i18n.en: We are all one man's sons; we are true men, thy servants are no spies.

paragraphs.commentary: The brothers' protest-formula deploys *kenim* (כֵּנִים), the substantival-plural of the adjective *ken* ('right, true, honest, upright'), used here in its rare nominalized sense of 'honest men, men of integrity'. The lexeme recurs five times across the chapter (vv 11, 19, 31, 33, 34) as the brothers' running self-designation — a chapter-internal refrain that ties the test-and-its-outcome together. ASV/KJV 'true men' (the archaic register that retains the lexical force of *ken* as 'integrity / uprightness'); NJPS / NRSV / Alter 'honest men' (modern register). The ASV-baseline is preserved for register-consistency across the chapter; the overlay entry [`kenim-true-men-honest-men-protest-formula-gen42`](#kenim-true-men-honest-men-protest-formula-gen42) documents the chapter-internal refrain and the rendering-options. See HALOT s.v. *ken* III; BDB p. 467.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֖אמֶר אֲלֵהֶ֑ם לֹ֕א כִּֽי־עֶרְוַ֥ת הָאָ֖רֶץ בָּאתֶ֥ם לִרְאֽוֹת׃

i18n.en: And he said unto them, Nay, but to see the nakedness of the land ye are come.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּאמְר֗וּ שְׁנֵ֣ים עָשָׂר֩ עֲבָדֶ֨יךָ אַחִ֧ים ׀ אֲנַ֛חְנוּ בְּנֵ֥י אִישׁ־אֶחָ֖ד בְּאֶ֣רֶץ כְּנָ֑עַן וְהִנֵּ֨ה הַקָּטֹ֤ן אֶת־אָבִ֙ינוּ֙ הַיּ֔וֹם וְהָאֶחָ֖ד אֵינֶֽנּוּ׃

i18n.en: And they said, We thy servants are twelve brethren, the sons of one man in the land of Kena'an; and, behold, the youngest is this day with our father, and one is not.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Ve-ha-echad einennu* — 'and one is not' — is the brothers' first deployment of the *einennu*-refrain that the chapter will repeat (v 32 the brothers; v 36 Ya'aqov twice, *Yosef einennu ve-Shim'on einennu*). The construction *einennu* (literally 'he is not' — the negative-existential particle with the 3ms suffix) is a charged euphemism: the brothers neither admit the sale nor state the conventional *met* ('dead' — Ya'aqov will be the one to say *met* at v 38). The refrain echoes Re'uven's anguished *ha-yeled einennu* at Gen 37:30 ('the child is not'), the moment Re'uven returned to the empty pit and discovered Yosef gone, and binds the chapter to Gen 37 across the missing-brother arc. The forward recurrence at 44:20 (the brothers retelling to Yosef: *ha-katan ha-yom et avinu ve-achiv met... ve-hu levado nishar*) and the laments at 44:26, 30 will continue the formula.

The ASV-baseline 'and one is not' (literal) preserves the construction's euphemistic force; NJPS 'and one is no more', Alter 'and one is no longer' are modern modulations. The overlay entry [`einennu-refrain-yosef-cycle-gen42`](#einennu-refrain-yosef-cycle-gen42) governs the chapter-internal refrain with cross-reference to Gen 37:30 and forward to Gen 44.

See Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 pp. 290-291; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 109; Alter *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 243 (on the *einennu* euphemism).

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר אֲלֵהֶ֖ם יוֹסֵ֑ף ה֗וּא אֲשֶׁ֨ר דִּבַּ֧רְתִּי אֲלֵכֶ֛ם לֵאמֹ֖ר מְרַגְּלִ֥ים אַתֶּֽם׃

i18n.en: And Yosef said unto them, That is it that I spake unto you, saying, Ye are spies:

paragraphs.text: בְּזֹ֖את תִּבָּחֵ֑נוּ חֵ֤י פַרְעֹה֙ אִם־תֵּצְא֣וּ מִזֶּ֔ה כִּ֧י אִם־בְּב֛וֹא אֲחִיכֶ֥ם הַקָּטֹ֖ן הֵֽנָּה׃

i18n.en: Hereby ye shall be proved: by the life of Pharaoh ye shall not go forth hence, except your youngest brother come hither.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Chei Par'oh* (חֵי פַרְעֹה) — 'by the life of Pharaoh' — is the formal oath-formula. The construction *chei + (royal/divine) name* swears by the continuing life of the named one, with the implicit force 'as surely as X lives, so surely will [the oath-content]'. The corpus parallel is *chei YHWH* ('as YHWH lives'), the predominant oath-formula on Israelite lips (Judg 8:19; 1 Sam 14:39, 45; 19:6; 20:3, 21; 25:26, 34; 26:10, 16; 28:10; 29:6; 2 Sam 4:9; 12:5; 14:11; 15:21; 1 Kgs 1:29; 2:24; 17:1, 12; 18:10, 15; 22:14; 2 Kgs 2:2, 4, 6; 3:14; 4:30; 5:16, 20; Jer 4:2; 5:2; 12:16; 16:14-15; 23:7-8; 38:16; 44:26; Hos 4:15; Ruth 3:13; 2 Chr 18:13). The *chei + king's-name* formula has documented ANE parallels (the swearing-by-the-king's-life as a standard court-oath, distinguishing the religious *chei YHWH* from the political *chei Par'oh*). Yosef's *chei Par'oh* is therefore registered as the appropriate court-oath of an Egyptian official — consistent with his current persona, distinct from the *chei YHWH* an Israelite character would use; the choice of formula is itself part of the maintained disguise. The oath recurs at v 16. ASV/KJV 'by the life of Pharaoh'; NJPS 'as Pharaoh lives'; Alter 'by Pharaoh's life'. The central entry [`chei-x-oath-by-the-life-formula`](#chei-x-oath-by-the-life-formula) governs the formula across the cluster.

See HALOT s.v. *chai*; BDB p. 311; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 291; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 520; for the ANE court-oath: M. R. Lehmann 'Biblical Oaths' ZAW 81 (1969) 74-92.

paragraphs.text: שִׁלְח֨וּ מִכֶּ֣ם אֶחָד֮ וְיִקַּ֣ח אֶת־אֲחִיכֶם֒ וְאַתֶּם֙ הֵאָ֣סְר֔וּ וְיִבָּֽחֲנוּ֙ דִּבְרֵיכֶ֔ם הַֽאֱמֶ֖ת אִתְּכֶ֑ם וְאִם־לֹ֕א חֵ֣י פַרְעֹ֔ה כִּ֥י מְרַגְּלִ֖ים אַתֶּֽם׃

i18n.en: Send one of you, and let him fetch your brother, and ye shall be bound, that your words may be proved, whether there be truth in you: or else by the life of Pharaoh surely ye are spies.

paragraphs.text: וַיֶּאֱסֹ֥ף אֹתָ֛ם אֶל־מִשְׁמָ֖ר שְׁלֹ֥שֶׁת יָמִֽים׃

i18n.en: And he put them all together into ward three days.

paragraphs.commentary: *Mishmar* (מִשְׁמָר), 'ward / custody', is the chapter's term for the place of detention; recurs at v 19 in the construct phrase *beit mishmarkhem* ('the house of your custody', 'your prison-house'). The lexeme is the general 'guard / custody / place-of-detention' term (cf. Gen 40:3-4, 7, where Yosef and the cupbearer/baker were held in the *mishmar* of the *sar ha-tabbachim* — the same office under which the Gen 39 *beit ha-sohar* falls). The chapter's *mishmar*/*beit mishmar* terminology may name the same facility as the Gen 39-40 *beit ha-sohar* (the round-house / prison) or a different one; ancient narrative does not distinguish, and modern translation cannot recover that distinction. ASV-baseline 'ward' (vv 17) / 'prison-house' (v 19) preserves the Hebrew's lexical-variation. The three-day detention is itself a marked literary period (Gen 22:4; 40:13, 19, 20; Hos 6:2; Jonah 2:1) — the threshold between captivity and resolution. The overlay entry [`mishmar-beit-mishmar-ward-prison-house-gen42`](#mishmar-beit-mishmar-ward-prison-house-gen42) governs the chapter-internal terminology, cross-referencing the central [`beit-ha-sohar-prison-round-house`](#beit-ha-sohar-prison-round-house). See HALOT s.v. *mishmar*; BDB p. 1038.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר אֲלֵהֶ֤ם יוֹסֵף֙ בַּיּ֣וֹם הַשְּׁלִישִׁ֔י זֹ֥את עֲשׂ֖וּ וִֽחְי֑וּ אֶת־הָאֱלֹהִ֖ים אֲנִ֥י יָרֵֽא׃

i18n.en: And Yosef said unto them the third day, This do, and live; for I fear Elohim:

paragraphs.commentary:
Yosef's *et ha-Elohim ani yarei* — 'I fear Elohim' (the formula *yir'at Elohim*, the Hebrew Bible's principal designation of moral restraint and covenantal-ethical conscience). The clause cross-references the central entry [`yirat-elohim-moral-restraint-motif`](#yirat-elohim-moral-restraint-motif), which is anchored at Gen 20:11 (Avraham's *raq ein yir'at Elohim ba-maqom ha-zeh*, his accusation that Gerar lacked the fear of Elohim) and Gen 22:12 (the Aqedah's *yere Elohim ata*). Gen 42:18 extends the chain: the *yir'at Elohim* formula on Yosef's lips in the foreign-court setting matches the Gen 20:11 register precisely — the morally-restrained presence in a foreign land — and reverses Avraham's pre-judgment: where Avraham assumed the Gerarites lacked the fear of Elohim, Yosef declares that he himself (the Egyptian-court official, by appearance) has it. The chain continues through Exod 1:17, 21 (the midwives), Exod 18:21 (Yitro), Exod 20:20, Lev 19:14 + 25:17, 36, 43, Deut 10:12, Job 1:1, Eccl 12:13, Prov 1:7 / 9:10. The central entry's appliesTo has been extended to include this verse.

The divine-name itself is *Elohim*, on Yosef's lips, continuing the Yosef-cycle Elohim-default that the overlay entry [`yosef-cycle-divine-name-alternation-yhwh-elohim`](#yosef-cycle-divine-name-alternation-yhwh-elohim) documents as the cycle's norm (against the Gen 39 YHWH-frame anomaly). The chapter's two Elohim-occurrences (v 18 and v 28) are both on characters' lips (Yosef here; the brothers at v 28); the narrator's voice deploys no divine name in the chapter — a sustained Elohim-only-on-character's-lips pattern. The overlay entry's appliesTo has been extended to include vv 18, 28.

The ASV-baseline 'for I fear Elohim' is preserved (KJV 'for I fear God'; the WoH 'Elohim' carrying the divine-name through per corpus convention).

See Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 291; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 110; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 521-522; on the *yir'at Elohim* motif at Gen 42:18, see J. Becker *Gottesfurcht im Alten Testament* 1965 (the foundational treatment).

paragraphs.text: אִם־כֵּנִ֣ים אַתֶּ֔ם אֲחִיכֶ֣ם אֶחָ֔ד יֵאָסֵ֖ר בְּבֵ֣ית מִשְׁמַרְכֶ֑ם וְאַתֶּם֙ לְכ֣וּ הָבִ֔יאוּ שֶׁ֖בֶר רַעֲב֥וֹן בָּתֵּיכֶֽם׃

i18n.en: If ye be true men, let one of your brethren be bound in your prison-house; but go ye, carry grain for the famine of your houses:

paragraphs.text: וְאֶת־אֲחִיכֶ֤ם הַקָּטֹן֙ תָּבִ֣יאוּ אֵלַ֔י וְיֵאָמְנ֥וּ דִבְרֵיכֶ֖ם וְלֹ֣א תָמ֑וּתוּ וַיַּעֲשׂוּ־כֵֽן׃

i18n.en: And bring your youngest brother unto me; so shall your words be verified, and ye shall not die. And they did so.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּאמְר֞וּ אִ֣ישׁ אֶל־אָחִ֗יו אֲבָל֮ אֲשֵׁמִ֣ים ׀ אֲנַחְנוּ֮ עַל־אָחִינוּ֒ אֲשֶׁ֨ר רָאִ֜ינוּ צָרַ֥ת נַפְשׁ֛וֹ בְּהִתְחַֽנְנ֥וֹ אֵלֵ֖ינוּ וְלֹ֣א שָׁמָ֑עְנוּ עַל־כֵּן֙ בָּ֣אָה אֵלֵ֔ינוּ הַצָּרָ֖ה הַזֹּֽאת׃

i18n.en: And they said one to another, We are verily guilty concerning our brother, in that we saw the distress of his soul, when he besought us, and we would not hear; therefore is this distress come upon us.

paragraphs.commentary:
**The brothers' moral reckoning.** *Aval ashemim anachnu al achinu* — 'we are verily guilty concerning our brother' — is the long-deferred reckoning for the Gen 37 sale. The emphatic particle *aval* ('truly, however, verily') is itself marked: in classical biblical Hebrew *aval* most often introduces an emphatic correction or an adversative-strong 'but truly' (cf. 2 Sam 14:5; 2 Kgs 4:14; Dan 10:7, 21; not yet the later 'however' of post-biblical Hebrew). The brothers acknowledge what they have not previously named.

The adjective/stative *ashem* (אָשֵׁם, plural *ashemim*) is a load-bearing HB lexeme: it names not merely 'guilt' as a feeling but the **objective state of bearing guilt-debt** — the standing condition of one who has incurred liability and must make it good. The cognate noun *asham* (אָשָׁם) is the technical 'guilt-offering' of the Levitical sacrificial system (Lev 5:6-7, 14-19; 6:6 [MT 5:25]; 7:1-7; 14:12-21; 19:21-22; Num 5:7-8 the 'restitution-with-twenty-percent-surcharge for *asham*' rule), the abstract noun for guilt-debt that the *asham*-sacrifice discharges. The verb *asham* — 'to incur guilt, bear guilt, suffer for guilt' — is pervasive in the prophetic literature (Hos 4:15; 5:15; 10:2; 13:1, 16; 14:1 [MT 14:2]; Joel 1:18; Ezek 6:6; 22:4; 25:12; Jer 2:3; 50:7; 51:5; Zech 11:5) and in the Psalter (Ps 5:11 [MT 5:10]; 34:22-23 [MT 34:22-23]). The substantival *ashemim* ('guilty ones') is rare and pointed: cf. 2 Sam 14:13. The Gen 42:21 verse is the **anchor** of the lexeme's cross-corpus reach into the Levitical guilt-offering system and the prophetic guilt-language. The central entry [`ashem-asham-guilt-bearing-vocabulary`](#ashem-asham-guilt-bearing-vocabulary) governs the cluster.

The brothers' confession deploys *tzarah* (צָרָה) twice — *tzarat nafsho* ('the distress of his soul', Yosef's anguish at the pit) and *ha-tzarah ha-zot* ('this distress', their own present plight). The repetition is a deliberate measure-for-measure: they recognise their present distress as the answering counterpart to the distress they once witnessed and ignored. The lexeme *tzarah* ('straitness, distress, trouble, anguish'; from *tzarar*, 'to be narrow / pressed') is one of the major HB lexemes for affliction; cross-corpus reach across Ps (Ps 9:10 [MT 9:9]; 22:12 [MT 22:11]; 25:17; 32:7; 34:18 [MT 34:17]; 37:39; 46:2 [MT 46:1]; 50:15; 54:9 [MT 54:7]; 71:20; 77:3 [MT 77:2]; 78:49; 81:8 [MT 81:7]; 86:7; 91:15; 107:6, 13, 19, 28; 116:3; 119:143; 120:1; 138:7; 142:3 [MT 142:2]); Isa 8:22; 26:16; 30:6; 33:2; 37:3; 46:7; 63:9; 65:16; Jer 4:31; 6:24; 14:8; 15:11; 16:19; 30:7 (the famous *eit tzarah hi le-Ya'aqov* — 'a time of tzarah it is for Ya'aqov', the prophetic-eschatological 'time of trouble for Jacob' that the chapter 42 grief anticipates lexically); 49:24; 50:43; Ezek 30:16; Hos 5:15; Obad 12, 14; Jonah 2:3 [MT 2:2]; Nah 1:7, 9; Hab 3:16; Zech 10:11; Prov 1:27; 11:8; 17:17; 24:10; 25:19. The central entry [`tzarah-distress-tribulation-vocabulary`](#tzarah-distress-tribulation-vocabulary) governs the lexeme; the entry is anchored at this verse with the prophetic-Psalmic cross-corpus reach.

ASV-baseline 'we are verily guilty' (preserving the emphatic *aval*) and 'distress' / 'distress' for the *tzarat nafsho* / *ha-tzarah ha-zot* pair preserves the lexical-echo the Hebrew builds; NJPS 'we are indeed guilty' / 'distress' / 'trouble'; NRSV 'we are guilty' / 'anguish' / 'anguish'; Alter 'in truth we are guilty' / 'distress'.

See HALOT s.v. *ashem* / *asham* and *tzarah*; BDB pp. 79-80 (*asham*) and 865 (*tzarah*); TDOT I:429-437 (*asham*) and XII:438-449 (*tzarah*); Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 291; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 pp. 110-111; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 522-523; on the *asham*-sacrifice system: J. Milgrom *Cult and Conscience: The* Asham *and the Priestly Doctrine of Repentance* SJLA 18, 1976; on the prophetic guilt-language: K. Koch '*ʾāšam* and *ʾāšām*' TDOT I:429-437; on Jer 30:7 and the 'time of trouble for Jacob': J. Bright *Jeremiah* AB 1965 pp. 273-279.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּעַן֩ רְאוּבֵ֨ן אֹתָ֜ם לֵאמֹ֗ר הֲלוֹא֩ אָמַ֨רְתִּי אֲלֵיכֶ֧ם ׀ לֵאמֹ֛ר אַל־תֶּחֶטְא֥וּ בַיֶּ֖לֶד וְלֹ֣א שְׁמַעְתֶּ֑ם וְגַם־דָּמ֖וֹ הִנֵּ֥ה נִדְרָֽשׁ׃

i18n.en: And Re'uven answered them, saying, Spake I not unto you, saying, Do not sin against the child; and ye would not hear? therefore also, behold, his blood is required.

paragraphs.commentary:
Re'uven invokes the Noachic blood-requiring principle by deploying the Niphal counterpart of the Gen 9:5 formula. *Ve-gam damo hinneh nidrash* — 'and behold, also his blood is required / sought / demanded' — uses *nidrash* (the Niphal of *darash*) in the specifically forensic-legal sense of divine reckoning for shed human blood. The central entry [`darosh-edrosh-dam`](#darosh-edrosh-dam) is anchored at Gen 9:5 (*et dimkhem le-nafshoteikhem edrosh ... edreshennu ... edrosh* — 'your blood, for your lives, will I demand ... I will demand it ... I will demand'), the active triple-iteration of the same root *d-r-sh*; the Gen 42:22 Niphal is the passive answer (the blood now *being* demanded). The central entry's appliesTo has been extended to include Gen 42:22. The Gen 4:10 *damei tzo'aqim* — *the bloods crying out from the ground* (central [`damei-tzo'aqim`](#damei-tzo'aqim)) — is the formula's prototype.

Re'uven's invocation of the Noachic blood-requiring covenant against his brothers (and, by implication, against himself — Re'uven was present at the sale, however unwillingly, Gen 37:21-22, 29-30) is a deliberate intertextual move. The chain Gen 4:10 (Hevel's blood crying out) → Gen 9:5 (the post-Flood standing rule of *edrosh*) → Gen 42:22 (Re'uven applying the rule to Yosef's presumed-shed blood) is one of the corpus's longest forensic-theological arcs; the cross-corpus continuation reaches Ezek 33:6 ('his blood I will require at the watchman's hand'); Ps 9:13 [MT 9:12] (*doresh damim... zakhar* — 'he who requires bloods ... remembers'); the prophetic blood-guilt material more broadly.

ASV-baseline 'behold, his blood is required' preserves the Niphal force; NJPS 'now comes the reckoning for his blood'; Alter 'and now his blood is requited' (paraphrasing). The lexical-echo to Gen 9:5 is decisive for preserving 'required'.

See HALOT s.v. *darash* (Niphal); BDB p. 205; TDOT III:293-307; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 291; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 111; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 523.

paragraphs.text: וְהֵם֙ לֹ֣א יָֽדְע֔וּ כִּ֥י שֹׁמֵ֖עַ יוֹסֵ֑ף כִּ֥י הַמֵּלִ֖יץ בֵּינֹתָֽם׃

i18n.en: And they knew not that Yosef understood them; for there was an interpreter between them.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Ha-melitz beinotam* — 'the interpreter between them' — uses *melitz* (מֵלִיץ) in the 'interpreter / translator' sense that is effectively a hapax in this register. The participle of the root *l-w-tz* is otherwise the 'scoffer / mocker' (Ps 1:1; Prov 9:7-8; 13:1; 14:6, 9; 15:12; 19:25, 29; 20:1; 21:11, 24; 22:10; 24:9), and in the Hiphil 'to scorn / deride' (Ps 119:51; Prov 14:9; 19:28); only here and at Job 33:23 (the 'mediating angel', *malakh melitz* — 'an angel, a mediator'), Isa 43:27 (*meliteikha pashe'u bi*, 'thy mediators / spokesmen / interpreters have transgressed against me'), and 2 Chr 32:31 (of the Babylonian envoys come to Hizqiyahu) is the sense 'interpreter / spokesman / mediator' attested. The Genesis occurrence is the earliest in the corpus and the only one denoting an unambiguous *court interpreter* (the others are mediator / spokesman / advocate registers).

The disclosure is the narrator's: the brothers, speaking unguardedly in Hebrew at v 21, do not know Yosef understands them — they assume the *melitz* is the only channel between them and the Egyptian official. Yosef's tears at v 24 (where he turns aside to weep) follow directly. The detail also serves the historical-verisimilitude function: Egyptian-court protocol used interpreters; Yosef, the *shallit*, would maintain the diplomatic fiction by routing his speech through a translator. The 'interpreter / dragoman' role is well-attested in ancient Near Eastern royal administration (cf. the Amarna letters; the *targumannu* class in Mesopotamian-court records).

The overlay entry [`melitz-interpreter-rare-sense-gen42`](#melitz-interpreter-rare-sense-gen42) governs the rare-sense lexeme. ASV-baseline 'for there was an interpreter between them' preserves the literal Hebrew word-order (*ki ha-melitz beinotam*); NJPS / NRSV / Alter likewise.

See HALOT s.v. *lutz* and *melitz*; BDB p. 539; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 291; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 111; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 523; on ANE court-interpreters: A. F. Rainey 'The Scribe at Ugarit' *Proceedings of the IAJS* 1969.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּסֹּ֥ב מֵֽעֲלֵיהֶ֖ם וַיֵּ֑בְךְּ וַיָּ֤שָׁב אֲלֵהֶם֙ וַיְדַבֵּ֣ר אֲלֵהֶ֔ם וַיִּקַּ֤ח מֵֽאִתָּם֙ אֶת־שִׁמְע֔וֹן וַיֶּאֱסֹ֥ר אֹת֖וֹ לְעֵינֵיהֶֽם׃

i18n.en: And he turned himself about from them, and wept; and he returned to them, and spake to them, and took Shim'on from among them, and bound him before their eyes.

paragraphs.commentary:
Yosef's first weeping (*va-yevk* — *and he wept*) is the first of seven Yosef-cycle weeping-occurrences (42:24; 43:30; 45:2, 14, 15; 46:29; 50:1, 17) — the cycle's recurring emotional-disclosure marker. The detail is private: Yosef *turns aside* (*va-yissov me-aleihem*) so the brothers do not see him weep, then composes himself (*va-yashov aleihem va-yedaber aleihem*) before continuing the test.

**The choice of Shim'on as hostage.** Of the ten brothers present, Yosef binds *Shim'on*. The choice is unmotivated at the surface but much-discussed in commentary as a deliberate literary echo. *Shim'on* (with Levi) was the architect of the Shechem-massacre at Gen 34 — the brothers' violence-pair — and Ya'aqov's deathbed-blessings will retrospectively condemn the pair at Gen 49:5-7 (*Shim'on ve-Levi achim, kelei chamas mekheroteihem* — 'Shim'on and Levi are brethren; weapons of violence are their swords'; *arur appam ki az ve-evratam ki qashatah* — 'cursed be their anger, for it was fierce; and their wrath, for it was cruel'). The literary reading — explicit in Sarna, Alter, Westermann, Sternberg, and the rabbinic tradition (Genesis Rabbah 91:8) — is that Yosef binds the brother whose violence-pattern most prefigured the violence done to himself. Re'uven, the firstborn (and the conventional hostage), is conspicuously *not* chosen — possibly because of his Gen 37:21-22 attempt to save Yosef (which v 22 has just recalled), possibly because of the Gen 35:22 deed that has placed him under the deathbed-blessings' first curse. The choice of Shim'on therefore reads as targeted: the brother most responsible for the original violence pays the chapter's most immediate cost.

The binding *le-eineihem* ('before their eyes') is also deliberate: the brothers must *see* the brother bound, just as Yosef once was bound (Gen 37:24, 28) — the visual measure-for-measure echoes the v 21 verbal one (they saw Yosef's *tzarat nafsho* and did not respond; now they see Shim'on bound and cannot intervene).

See Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 291; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 pp. 111-112; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 523-524; Sternberg *The Poetics of Biblical Narrative* 1985 ch. 9; Alter *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 244; for the rabbinic tradition on Shim'on-as-hostage: *Genesis Rabbah* 91:8; Rashi ad loc.

paragraphs.text: וַיְצַ֣ו יוֹסֵ֗ף וַיְמַלְא֣וּ אֶת־כְּלֵיהֶם֮ בָּר֒ וּלְהָשִׁ֤יב כַּסְפֵּיהֶם֙ אִ֣ישׁ אֶל־שַׂקּ֔וֹ וְלָתֵ֥ת לָהֶ֛ם צֵדָ֖ה לַדָּ֑רֶךְ וַיַּ֥עַשׂ לָהֶ֖ם כֵּֽן׃

i18n.en: Then Yosef commanded to fill their vessels with grain, and to restore every man's money into his sack, and to give them provisions for the way: and thus was it done unto them.

paragraphs.commentary:
The verse introduces the chapter's sack-vocabulary alternation. *Keleihem* ('their vessels', *kelim* — the general 'utensils / vessels / equipment / containers') is the first term; *saqo* ('his sack', *saq* — the specific cloth-bag) is the second. v 27 will introduce a third term, *amtachat* (אַמְתַּחַת) — also 'sack', but a lexeme confined within the HB to the Gen 42-44 grain-purchase narrative (Gen 42:27, 28; 43:12, 18, 21, 22, 23; 44:1, 2, 8, 11, 12). The three-term alternation (*kelim* / *saq* / *amtachat*) is striking and admits several explanations: (a) the lexemes denote different containers (the *kelim* being travel-vessels, the *saq* the bag, the *amtachat* a sub-pouch within the bag — supporting v 27's 'in the *mouth* of his *amtachat*' and v 35's 'his bundle of money in his *saq*' as referring to distinct compartments); (b) the alternation is stylistic synonymy without referential differentiation; (c) source-critical seams (some commentators have read the *saq*/*amtachat* alternation as a J/E split). ASV/KJV render variously 'vessels' (v 25 *kelim*), 'sack' (v 25 *saq*, v 27 *saq*, v 27/28 *amtachat*, v 35 *saq*), flattening the distinction. The overlay entry [`kelim-sak-amtachat-sack-vocabulary-alternation-gen42-44`](#kelim-sak-amtachat-sack-vocabulary-alternation-gen42-44) governs the alternation across the Gen 42-44 arc, preserving the ASV-baseline surface-rendering while documenting the lexical-distinctness observation.

The *kesef* (silver / money) returned to each man's sack is the chapter's pivot from test to providence: Yosef has commanded the silver-restitution as an act of grace (the brothers will receive grain without final cost), but the brothers will read the restitution as a trap (vv 28, 35). The unresolved gap between Yosef's intention and the brothers' reading drives the second-journey arc through Gen 43.

See HALOT s.v. *kelim*, *saq*, *amtachat*; BDB pp. 479 (*kelim*), 974 (*saq*), 607 (*amtachat*); Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 292; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 112; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 524; on the *amtachat* lexeme's restriction to Gen 42-44: BDB p. 607 (noting the singular distribution).

paragraphs.text: וַיִּשְׂא֥וּ אֶת־שִׁבְרָ֖ם עַל־חֲמֹרֵיהֶ֑ם וַיֵּלְכ֖וּ מִשָּֽׁם׃

i18n.en: And they laded their asses with their grain, and departed thence.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּפְתַּ֨ח הָאֶחָ֜ד אֶת־שַׂקּ֗וֹ לָתֵ֥ת מִסְפּ֛וֹא לַחֲמֹר֖וֹ בַּמָּל֑וֹן וַיַּרְא֙ אֶת־כַּסְפּ֔וֹ וְהִנֵּה־ה֖וּא בְּפִ֥י אַמְתַּחְתּֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: And as one of them opened his sack to give his ass provender in the lodging-place, he espied his money; and, behold, it was in the mouth of his sack.

paragraphs.commentary:
The verse alternates *saq* (the bag the brother opens) and *amtachat* (the sack-pouch within which the money was placed, at its 'mouth') — a precise lexical-differentiation in a single sentence. The reading 'in the mouth of his *amtachat*' (*be-fi amtachto*) presupposes the *amtachat* as a distinct container with an identifiable opening.

*Ba-malon* — 'in the lodging-place' (מָלוֹן) — uses the noun *malon* for the place of overnighting on the journey. The lexeme recurs at Gen 43:21 (the brothers' return-journey *malon*), Exod 4:24 (the bridegroom-of-blood encounter at the *malon*), Josh 4:3, 8 (the *malon* of the night), 2 Kgs 19:23 = Isa 37:24, Jer 9:1 [MT 9:2] (a wayfarers' lodge). The 'lodging-place' here is presumably a caravanserai or the camp-site for the night on the return journey; it is not an 'inn' in the modern sense (the KJV's 'inn' is anachronistic — caravanserai-style way-stations were the actual institutions). ASV-baseline 'lodging-place'; NJPS / NRSV likewise; Alter 'night camp'. The overlay entry [`malon-lodging-place-wayfaring-stopover-gen42`](#malon-lodging-place-wayfaring-stopover-gen42) governs the lexeme with cross-corpus reach noted.

See HALOT s.v. *malon*; BDB p. 533; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 292; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 524; on ANE wayfaring-stopovers: V. H. Matthews 'Hospitality and Hostility in Judges 4' BTB 21 (1991) 13-21.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר אֶל־אֶחָיו֙ הוּשַׁ֣ב כַּסְפִּ֔י וְגַ֖ם הִנֵּ֣ה בְאַמְתַּחְתִּ֑י וַיֵּצֵ֣א לִבָּ֗ם וַיֶּֽחֶרְד֞וּ אִ֤ישׁ אֶל־אָחִיו֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר מַה־זֹּ֛את עָשָׂ֥ה אֱלֹהִ֖ים לָֽנוּ׃

i18n.en: And he said unto his brethren, My money is restored; and, lo, it is even in my sack: and their heart failed them, and they turned trembling one to another, saying, What is this that Elohim hath done unto us?

paragraphs.commentary:
*Va-yetze libbam* — literally 'and their heart went out' — is the chapter's striking physiological-emotional idiom for the sudden onset of dread. The construction 'the heart goes out' is rare in the HB (the closest parallel is Cant 5:6, *nafshi yatz'ah ve-dabro*, 'my soul went out at his speaking' — also a sudden-shock register; Gen 45:26 has a related but distinct idiom *va-yafag libbo*, 'his heart fainted', of Ya'aqov on hearing Yosef lives). The idiom conveys courage / life-force draining away — the heart, as the seat of resolve, 'going out' of them. ASV/KJV 'their heart failed them'; NJPS / Alter 'their hearts sank'; the literal 'their heart went out' is preserved-in-spirit by the ASV-baseline. The overlay entry [`yetze-libbam-heart-failed-idiom-gen42`](#yetze-libbam-heart-failed-idiom-gen42) governs the chapter-singular idiom.

The brothers' question — *mah zot asah Elohim lanu* ('what is this that Elohim hath done unto us') — is the chapter's second Elohim-on-character's-lips occurrence, answering Yosef's *et ha-Elohim ani yarei* at v 18. Both characters in the chapter who name the deity name *Elohim*; both do so in the moral-providential register; both within the Egyptian setting. The narrator's voice deploys no divine name in the chapter at all — a sustained Elohim-only-on-character's-lips pattern that the overlay entry [`yosef-cycle-divine-name-alternation-yhwh-elohim`](#yosef-cycle-divine-name-alternation-yhwh-elohim) tracks across the cycle (the Gen 39 YHWH-frame is the documented anomaly; Gen 40-41 and now Gen 42 confirm the cycle's Elohim-norm). The overlay entry's appliesTo has been extended to include vv 18, 28.

Note also the brothers' attribution: they read the restored silver as a divine act — *Elohim hath done [this] unto us* — not as the act of the *shallit* whose silver it actually is. The chapter's pattern of moral-providential reading (the brothers seeing in their plight the Gen 37 reckoning at v 21; reading the silver as Elohim's act here) is one of the cycle's running theological-literary observations: the brothers see Elohim acting through circumstance even when Yosef is the proximate agent. Gen 45:5, 7, 8 will be Yosef's own reformulation of the same pattern (*lo attem shelachtem oti hennah ki ha-Elohim* — 'not you sent me here, but Elohim').

See HALOT s.v. *yatza* (the heart-idiom); BDB p. 422; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 292; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 113; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 525; Alter *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 245.

paragraphs.text: וַיָּבֹ֛אוּ אֶל־יַעֲקֹ֥ב אֲבִיהֶ֖ם אַ֣רְצָה כְּנָ֑עַן וַיַּגִּ֣ידוּ ל֔וֹ אֵ֛ת כָּל־הַקֹּרֹ֥ת אֹתָ֖ם לֵאמֹֽר׃

i18n.en: And they came unto Ya'aqov their father unto the land of Kena'an, and told him all that had befallen them, saying,

paragraphs.text: דִּ֠בֶּר הָאִ֨ישׁ אֲדֹנֵ֥י הָאָ֛רֶץ אִתָּ֖נוּ קָשׁ֑וֹת וַיִּתֵּ֣ן אֹתָ֔נוּ כִּֽמְרַגְּלִ֖ים אֶת־הָאָֽרֶץ׃

i18n.en: The man, the lord of the land, spake roughly with us, and took us for spies of the country.

paragraphs.commentary: The brothers' retelling begins, deploying the same adverbial *qashot* ('roughly / harshly') the narrator used at v 7. *Ha-ish adonei ha-aretz* ('the man, the lord of the land') is a respectful periphrasis — they will not name him (he has no name to them yet) and use the formal *adonei ha-aretz* ('lord of the land') in place of the technical *shallit* of v 6 (which the narrator used but the brothers would not have heard as a title). The retelling-variation across vv 30-34 (compared to vv 9-20) is a deliberate literary device — Sarna and Alter both note the discreet edits the brothers make in their account to Ya'aqov (notably the suppression of the Shim'on-binding spectacle's vividness and the diplomatic softening of Yosef's *spies* accusation).

paragraphs.text: וַנֹּ֥אמֶר אֵלָ֖יו כֵּנִ֣ים אֲנָ֑חְנוּ לֹ֥א הָיִ֖ינוּ מְרַגְּלִֽים׃

i18n.en: And we said unto him, We are true men; we are no spies:

paragraphs.text: שְׁנֵים־עָשָׂ֥ר אֲנַ֛חְנוּ אַחִ֖ים בְּנֵ֣י אָבִ֑ינוּ הָאֶחָ֣ד אֵינֶ֔נּוּ וְהַקָּטֹ֥ן הַיּ֛וֹם אֶת־אָבִ֖ינוּ בְּאֶ֥רֶץ כְּנָֽעַן׃

i18n.en: We are twelve brethren, sons of our father; one is not, and the youngest is this day with our father in the land of Kena'an.

paragraphs.commentary: The second occurrence of the chapter's *einennu* refrain (*ha-echad einennu*, 'one is not') — the brothers repeating to Ya'aqov the formula they used to the disguised Yosef at v 13. Ya'aqov will pick up the formula and double it at v 36 (*Yosef einennu ve-Shim'on einennu*).

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֵלֵ֗ינוּ הָאִישׁ֙ אֲדֹנֵ֣י הָאָ֔רֶץ בְּזֹ֣את אֵדַ֔ע כִּ֥י כֵנִ֖ים אַתֶּ֑ם אֲחִיכֶ֤ם הָֽאֶחָד֙ הַנִּ֣יחוּ אִתִּ֔י וְאֶת־רַעֲב֥וֹן בָּתֵּיכֶ֖ם קְח֥וּ וָלֵֽכוּ׃

i18n.en: And the man, the lord of the land, said unto us, Hereby shall I know that ye are true men: leave one of your brethren with me, and take grain for the famine of your houses, and go your way;

paragraphs.text: וְ֠הָבִיאוּ אֶת־אֲחִיכֶ֣ם הַקָּטֹן֮ אֵלַי֒ וְאֵֽדְעָ֗ה כִּ֣י לֹ֤א מְרַגְּלִים֙ אַתֶּ֔ם כִּ֥י כֵנִ֖ים אַתֶּ֑ם אֶת־אֲחִיכֶם֙ אֶתֵּ֣ן לָכֶ֔ם וְאֶת־הָאָ֖רֶץ תִּסְחָֽרוּ׃

i18n.en: and bring your youngest brother unto me: then shall I know that ye are no spies, but that ye are true men: so will I deliver you your brother, and ye shall traffic in the land.

paragraphs.text: וַיְהִ֗י הֵ֚ם מְרִיקִ֣ים שַׂקֵּיהֶ֔ם וְהִנֵּה־אִ֥ישׁ צְרוֹר־כַּסְפּ֖וֹ בְּשַׂקּ֑וֹ וַיִּרְא֞וּ אֶת־צְרֹר֧וֹת כַּסְפֵּיהֶ֛ם הֵ֥מָּה וַאֲבִיהֶ֖ם וַיִּירָֽאוּ׃

i18n.en: And it came to pass as they emptied their sacks, that, behold, every man's bundle of money was in his sack: and when they and their father saw their bundles of money, they were afraid.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Tzeror kesef* (צְרוֹר כֶּסֶף) — 'bundle of money / bag of silver' — uses the noun *tzeror* ('bundle, pouch, bag', from *tzarar* 'to bind up / tie in a bundle') for the small money-pouches in which silver was carried. The lexeme's cross-corpus distribution: 1 Sam 25:29 (the famous *tzeror ha-chayim*, 'bundle of the living' — Avigail's blessing of David: *ve-haitah nefesh adoni tzerurah be-tzeror ha-chayim et YHWH Elohekha*, 'the soul of my lord shall be bound up in the bundle of the living with YHWH thy Elohim' — the poetic-theological 'bound up in the bundle of life' that has entered Jewish liturgical-funerary use); Prov 7:20 (the *tzeror ha-kesef*, 'bag of money', the adulteress's husband took on his journey — strikingly the same idiom as here, the merchant's traveling-pouch); Hag 1:6 (the holed pouch — *tzeror naquv*); Cant 1:13 (*tzeror ha-mor*, 'bundle / sachet of myrrh'). The Genesis 42 occurrence is the earliest mercantile *tzeror kesef* in the corpus; the overlay entry [`tzeror-kesef-bundle-of-money-pouch-gen42`](#tzeror-kesef-bundle-of-money-pouch-gen42) governs the chapter occurrence with the cross-corpus reach documented as a promotion-path. ASV/KJV 'bundle of money' (the literal *tzeror* preserved); NJPS 'money-bag'; NRSV 'bag of money'; Alter 'bundle of silver'.

The sight of the silver-bundles is the final shock — what one brother discovered at the *malon* (v 27-28) the others now confirm at home. The verse closes with *va-yir'a'u* (the simple verb of fear: 'they were afraid') — Ya'aqov's first registration of dread on this episode, which his speech at v 36 will articulate.

See HALOT s.v. *tzarar* and *tzeror*; BDB p. 865; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 292; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 526.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר אֲלֵהֶם֙ יַעֲקֹ֣ב אֲבִיהֶ֔ם אֹתִ֖י שִׁכַּלְתֶּ֑ם יוֹסֵ֤ף אֵינֶ֙נּוּ֙ וְשִׁמְע֣וֹן אֵינֶ֔נּוּ וְאֶת־בִּנְיָמִ֣ן תִּקָּ֔חוּ עָלַ֖י הָי֥וּ כֻלָּֽנָה׃

i18n.en: And Ya'aqov their father said unto them, Me have ye bereaved of my children: Yosef is not, and Shim'on is not, and ye will take Binyamin away: all these things are against me.

paragraphs.commentary:
**Ya'aqov's *shikkaltem* — the deepest grief-term of the cycle.** *Oti shikkaltem* — 'me ye have bereaved [of my children]' — uses the Piel of *shakhol* (שׁכל) in its active-causative sense: 'to bereave [someone] of their children, to render childless'. The Piel form names a specific kind of grief — not generic mourning but the bereavement of children, the loss-of-progeny that severs the line. This is one of the deepest grief-lexemes in the HB and is structurally marked in Genesis: it appeared first at Gen 27:45 in Rivkah's *lammah eshkal gam shneikhem yom echad* — 'why should I be bereaved of you both also in one day' (the only previous Genesis occurrence, in Rivkah's instruction to Ya'aqov to flee Esav, prefiguring her fear of losing both sons to Esav's wrath); Ya'aqov will repeat the lexeme at Gen 43:14 in *ve-ani ka'asher shakholti shakhalti* ('and if I am bereaved, I am bereaved'), the resigned acceptance-formula of the second-journey arc. The Gen 27:45 → 42:36 → 43:14 sequence forms a cross-Genesis bereavement-arc, the matriarch's fear of double-bereavement (Gen 27:45) answered a generation later by the patriarch's accusation of double-bereavement (Gen 42:36).

The lexeme's cross-corpus reach is one of the corpus's grief-theology cores: Lev 26:22 (the covenant-curse *ve-shikkalah etkhem* — 'and [the wild beasts] shall bereave you' — the bereavement-by-wild-beast covenantal curse); Deut 32:25 (the Song of Mosheh's *gam bachur gam betulah yonek im ish seivah* — 'both young man and virgin, suckling with the gray-haired man', the comprehensive-bereavement formula, lexically related); Jer 15:7; 18:21 (the 'bereave them of children' prayer-curse); Hos 9:12, 14 (the prophetic bereavement-formula: 'though they bring up their children, yet I will bereave them, that there shall not be a man left'); Ezek 5:17; 14:15; 36:13-14 (the land *meshakkelet* — 'bereaver of [her people]'); Lam 1:20. The lexeme is the standard prophetic-covenantal threat for bereavement-as-judgment. The central entry [`shakhol-bereavement-of-children-vocabulary`](#shakhol-bereavement-of-children-vocabulary) governs the cluster, anchored at the Gen 27:45 → 42:36 → 43:14 cross-Genesis arc and extensible to the prophetic-covenantal cross-corpus.

**The *einennu* refrain's climactic deployment.** Ya'aqov doubles the formula: *Yosef einennu ve-Shim'on einennu* — 'Yosef is not, and Shim'on is not'. The refrain that the brothers used twice (vv 13, 32) becomes the patriarch's lament, applied to two brothers at once (Yosef presumed dead; Shim'on bound in Mitsrayim) and threatened toward a third (Binyamin). The formula's chapter-internal arc — brothers (v 13) → brothers retelling (v 32) → Ya'aqov twice doubled (v 36) → forward to 44:20, 26, 30 (the brothers' arc, again to a foreign official) — is one of the cycle's deepest literary structures. The closing *alai hayu khullanah* ('all these things are against me') seals the lament register.

ASV/KJV 'me have ye bereaved of my children' (the dative-of-disadvantage *oti* preserved); NJPS 'It is always me that you bereave'; NRSV 'I am the one you have bereaved of my children'; Alter 'me you have bereaved'.

See HALOT s.v. *shakhol* (Piel); BDB p. 1013; TDOT XV:11-15; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 292; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 pp. 113-114; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 526; Alter *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 245; on the bereavement-of-children covenantal curse: D. R. Hillers *Treaty-Curses and the Old Testament Prophets* BibOr 16, 1964; on the cross-Genesis *shakhol* arc Gen 27:45 → 42:36 → 43:14: J. P. Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* SSN 17, 1975.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר רְאוּבֵן֙ אֶל־אָבִ֣יו לֵאמֹ֔ר אֶת־שְׁנֵ֤י בָנַי֙ תָּמִ֔ית אִם־לֹ֥א אֲבִיאֶ֖נּוּ אֵלֶ֑יךָ תְּנָ֤ה אֹתוֹ֙ עַל־יָדִ֔י וַאֲנִ֖י אֲשִׁיבֶ֥נּוּ אֵלֶֽיךָ׃

i18n.en: And Re'uven spake unto his father, saying, Slay my two sons, if I bring him not to thee: deliver him into my hand, and I will bring him to thee again.

paragraphs.commentary:
Re'uven's offer — *et shenei vanai tamit im lo avi'enu eleikha* — is morally extreme and rhetorically tone-deaf: he offers Ya'aqov the slaughter of two grandsons as guarantee against the loss of a son. Ya'aqov will refuse (v 38) without responding to the offer's terms directly. The Re'uven-Ya'aqov exchange contrasts pointedly with the Yehudah-Ya'aqov exchange of Gen 43:8-10, where Yehudah will offer himself (*anokhi e'ervennu* — 'I will be surety for him') as the guarantor — the offered-self rather than the offered-grandchildren. The narrative is sorting the brothers' leadership-claims; Yehudah's offer in ch 43 will succeed where Re'uven's fails here.

The Re'uven offer is also the closing instance of Re'uven's recurring narrative-function: the well-intentioned firstborn whose interventions consistently miss the mark (Gen 35:22 the Bilhah deed undermining his firstborn-claim; Gen 37:21-22 the failed attempt to save Yosef; here the grandson-slaughter offer). The Gen 49:3-4 deathbed verdict — *pachaz ka-mayim, al totar* ('unstable as water, thou shalt not have the pre-eminence') — is foreshadowed by this exchange.

See Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 292; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 114; Alter *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 246.

i18n.en: And he said, My son shall not go down with you; for his brother is dead, and he only is left: if harm befall him by the way in which ye go, then will ye bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to She'ol.

paragraphs.commentary:
**Ya'aqov's accepted-as-fact death of Yosef.** *Ki achiv met ve-hu levaddo nishar* — 'for his brother is dead, and he only is left'. The patriarch states as flat fact (*met*, 'dead') what is in fact false — the chapter's deepest irony. The brothers (and the reader) know Yosef lives; Ya'aqov, who has accepted the Gen 37:33 evidence (the bloodied tunic) and is unaware of the v 6 *shallit*, speaks of Yosef in the past-tense closure of mourning. The clause *ve-hu levaddo nishar* ('and he alone is left') identifies Binyamin as the sole-surviving son of Rachel (cf. Gen 35:24, the two Rachel-sons), a Rachel-line-extinction fear; the phrase will recur at 44:20 (in the brothers' retelling, *va-yivvater hu levaddo le-immo*, 'he alone is left of his mother').

**The repeated *ason*-formula.** *U-kra'ahu ason ba-derekh* — 'and harm befall him by the way' — repeats the v 4 *ason* formula. *Ason* is Ya'aqov's marked fear-term, deployed only of Binyamin and only in the Yosef-cycle journeys (Gen 42:4, 38; 44:29). The cross-corpus parallel at Exod 21:22-23 fixes the lethal force (the *ason*/no-*ason* distinction in the law of injury to a pregnant woman names fatal vs non-fatal outcomes). The overlay entry [`ason-fatal-mischance-yaaqov-fear-formula-gen42`](#ason-fatal-mischance-yaaqov-fear-formula-gen42) governs both occurrences (consistent with v 4).

**The *seivah* + She'olah descent-formula.** *Ve-horadtem et seivati be-yagon She'olah* — 'and ye shall bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to She'ol' — is the chapter's striking concrete embodiment of Ya'aqov's aged-mourning. *Seivah* (שֵׂיבָה), from *sav* ('gray-haired one, elder'), is the metonymic noun for 'old age, gray-haired age'; the lexeme recurs at Gen 15:15 (Avraham's *seivah tovah*, 'a good old age'), Gen 25:8 (Avraham's death at *seivah tovah*), 1 Kgs 2:6, 9 (Shim'i's *seivah*), Lev 19:32 (the honoring-the-aged formula *mipnei seivah taqum* — 'before the *seivah* thou shalt rise up'), Prov 16:31 (*atzeret tif'eret seivah* — 'the gray head is a crown of glory'), Prov 20:29. The overlay entry [`seivah-gray-hairs-old-age-yaaqov-yosef-cycle`](#seivah-gray-hairs-old-age-yaaqov-yosef-cycle) governs the lexeme as deployed in the Yosef-cycle laments; the phrase *seivati ... She'olah* will recur at Gen 44:29, 31.

**The She'ol-descent formula recurs.** *She'olah* — the directional / locative form 'down to She'ol' — is the exact recurrence of Ya'aqov's Gen 37:35 *ki ered el beni avel She'olah* ('for I will go down to She'ol unto my son mourning'), and the chapter's final line lands on the same descent-to-She'ol grief-formula that opened the cycle's mourning at Gen 37:35. The central entry [`sheol-underworld-realm-of-the-dead`](#sheol-underworld-realm-of-the-dead) has had its appliesTo extended to include Gen 42:38 (and the forward 44:29, 44:31 occurrences when those chapters are translated). The Ya'aqov-internal *seivah* + She'olah descent-formula across the cycle (Gen 37:35, 42:38, 44:29, 44:31) is one of the deepest grief-arcs in the corpus.

**The dramatic irony intensifies.** The chapter that opened with Ya'aqov sending the brothers down to Mitsrayim closes with Ya'aqov refusing to send the last Rachel-son down — and the patriarch's accepted-as-fact death of Yosef stands as the chapter's final ironic note. Ya'aqov has fully accepted as fact what is in fact false; the brothers (and reader) know better; the reconciliation that will eventually undo the false closure is still chapters away. The chapter ends in deadlock — Ya'aqov refusing, the brothers unable to return for Shim'on without Binyamin, the famine still ahead. The deadlock will hold through Gen 43:1-2 ('the famine was sore in the land'), where renewed need will force the question open again.

See HALOT s.v. *seivah*, *ason*, *she'ol*; BDB pp. 966 (*seivah*), 62 (*ason*), 982 (*she'ol*); Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 pp. 292-293; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 pp. 114-115; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 527-528; Alter *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 246; on the *seivah* + She'olah grief-formula across the cycle: J. P. Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* SSN 17, 1975; on the dramatic irony of Ya'aqov's accepted-as-fact closure: Sternberg *The Poetics of Biblical Narrative* 1985 ch. 9.
